subject: Private endpoint egress: IP escrow proposal, SNI/TLS fingerprint guidance, and operator SLOs
messages:
From: Arjun Shah <arjun.shah@acmehealth.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Priya Gupta <priya.gupta@acmehealth.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Jun 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Request: provenance and attestations for private endpoint egress

Marissa —

Thanks for the walkthrough yesterday. Our security team has a few follow-ups before we can sign off on the private connector for production:

1) Provenance for egress IPs: we need an auditable ledger showing which IPs are used for outbound connections from our private runtime (including timestamps and any ownership/lease info). Will you provide an exportable artifact we can retain for audits?

2) TLS/SNI fingerprinting: our perimeter inspects SNI and TLS fingerprints for upstream vetting. Can you confirm the stability of SNI values and whether Redwood can provide guidance or fingerprints we can match against?

3) Operator SLAs and rotation windows: what is your recommended rotation cadence for ephemeral IPs and how do you notify customers when an egress pool changes?

4) Escrow/attestation model: as a regulated customer, we prefer either (a) a time-stamped IP escrow delivered to us, or (b) a cryptographically-signed snapshot we can verify later. Any preferences or constraints on Redwood's side?

We'd like a short response that we can take back to our compliance team today — ideally with an artefact or link we can reference.

Thanks,
Arjun Shah
Security Operations
Acme Health

(Attachment request: any ledger/guide would be great)

Subject: Re: Request: provenance and attestations for private endpoint egress

Arjun —

Thanks for the clear list. High-level answers below and I've looped in our network and ops leads for details and acceptance criteria. I'm attaching two artifacts for your team: a time‑stamped IP ledger (egress-ip-ledger.xlsx) and a short SNI/TLS fingerprinting guide (sni-tls-fingerprint-guide.pdf). Both are snapshots we generate at the time of handoff; we can produce these on a weekly cadence or on-demand for audits.

Quick answers:
- Provenance: Redwood Private runtimes can egress through either (1) a customer-attached NAT/gateway you control, or (2) Redwood-managed egress pools (recommended when customers use our control plane routing). For option (2) we maintain a ledger that records: assigned IP, allocation start/end timestamps, region, and assignment token. The attached XLSX is an example export.

- SNI/TLS fingerprinting: we do not mutate SNI. For hosted control-plane egress, SNI values are stable per service host (e.g., api.redwood.ai). We publish a short fingerprinting guide — included — that lists SNI names and the TLS cert chain identifiers we see when calling from our egress. If you require cryptographic attestations beyond this (e.g., signed cert transparency proofs), we can discuss an add-on.

- Rotation & notification: our default rotation for ephemeral egress IPs is 24–72 hours for high-security pools and 7–14 days for low-churn pools. We update the ledger at every rotation and can push a signed snapshot to a customer S3 / secure Share link. For production acceptance we recommend you require: (a) a snapshot within the last 24 hours at cutover, and (b) webhook notifications of pool change during sensitive windows.

- Escrow model: we support time-stamped CSV/XLSX exports that you can store (option A). Option B is a signed JSON manifest (HMAC + timestamp) that we can deliver and you can verify offline. For regulated customers we often do both.

Action items I propose:
1) Internal: David / Ben / Stephanie to capture the operational SLOs and propose rotation windows.
2) External: Arjun / Priya — confirm which escrow format you prefer (XLSX + HMACed manifest, or another).
3) We'll schedule a 30‑minute follow-up to align on acceptance criteria and delivery endpoints.

Attachments: egress-ip-ledger.xlsx (sample ledger), sni-tls-fingerprint-guide.pdf

Best,
Marissa Cole
Manager, Customer Solutions — Redwood Inference

Looping in operational specifics and acceptance criteria from the runtime/NOC side.

Summary of proposed SLOs & ops behaviors (for Acme review):
- IP assignment model: allocate from a labeled pool (e.g., acme-prod-usw2). Every allocation is an entry in the ledger with start_ts/end_ts and assignment_id.
- Rotation windows: configurable per-pool. Default: 72h for medium-security, 24h for high-security. Low-churn (static) pools can be pinned for 30 days with approval.
- Notification: we provide a webhook + signed manifest push at rotation time. Manifest includes new_ip_list, retired_ips, rotation_ts, and a HMAC signature.
- Audit & escrow: deliverables can be (a) a time-stamped XLSX placed in your S3 bucket, (b) an optional signed manifest to your KMS-protected endpoint.
- NAT behavior & egress NAT mapping: we will provide a CIDR->IP mapping excerpt and example connection trace (src_port, dst_host, tls_sni, egress_ip) for sample calls to your test endpoints so you can validate matching fingerprints.

Acceptance criteria for cutover (suggested):
1) Acme validates SNI/TLS fingerprints against our sample trace for 3 consecutive calls.
2) Acme verifies receipt and signature of the ledger snapshot in their S3 test bucket.
3) A 48-hour monitoring window post-cutover where Redwood will not rotate high-security pool IPs unless an ops emergency occurs (to give Acme time to confirm allowlisting).

Linking to the implementation ticket: JIRA-RED-1247 for the webhook + manifest work (internal only).

Notes: Ben — can you confirm the default HMAC algorithm we will use (sha256) and whether we should sign manifests with our platform key or via KMS export for Acme?

-D
David Kim
